title: Heaps
summary: A heap keeps the smallest (or largest) value at the root of an array-backed tree. Push and pop cost O(log n) each, so it is the tool whenever you keep asking for the current best.
idea: Push sifts a value up past bigger parents; pop moves the last value to the root and sifts it down. The best value is always at index 0.

signals.see: You keep asking for the smallest or largest item while items are still being added.
signals.think: Use a heap. Peeking is O(1), and each push or pop is O(log n). Sorting again after each change would be O(n log n).

signals.see: The question asks for the k largest, k smallest or k most frequent items.
signals.think: Keep a heap of size k. See the Top K page.

signals.see: You must merge several sorted lists, or always take the next earliest event.
signals.think: Put the front of each list in a heap. See the K-way merge page.

signals.see: You need a running median or a balance between a lower and an upper half.
signals.think: Use a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. See the Two heaps page.

phrasings: A hospital triage desk always treats the most urgent patient waiting, while new patients keep arriving.
A game repeatedly smashes the two heaviest rocks together. What is left at the end?
A scheduler must always run the job with the earliest deadline next.

picture.title: Keep only the best at the top
picture.alt: On the left, the whole list is sorted again after every insert, which costs O(n log n) each time. On the right, a heap sifts the new value up one path and keeps the best value at the root, costing O(log n).
picture.caption: A heap only fixes one root-to-leaf path per push or pop.

code.py:
def heap_sort(nums):
    heap, out = [], []  #@init
    for x in nums:
        heap.append(x); i = len(heap) - 1  #@push
        while i > 0 and heap[(i - 1) // 2] > heap[i]:  #@up
            p = (i - 1) // 2; heap[i], heap[p] = heap[p], heap[i]; i = p  #@swapup
    while heap:  #@pop
        out.append(heap[0])  #@take
        last = heap.pop()
        if not heap: break
        heap[0] = last; i = 0  #@move
        while True:
            small = min((c for c in (i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2) if c < len(heap)), key=lambda c: heap[c])  #@down
            if small == i: break
            heap[i], heap[small] = heap[small], heap[i]; i = small  #@swapdown
    return out  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 10 whole numbers between -99 and 99, separated by commas or spaces.

oneLiner: push: append, sift up while parent > x; pop: move last to root, sift down to the smaller child

exercise.prompt: Each turn, take the two heaviest stones, with weights a ≥ b. If a = b both are destroyed; otherwise a stone of weight a − b goes back. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0 if none is left. The starter uses a min-heap as it is, so it smashes the two lightest stones instead.
hints: You need the two largest values again and again while new values arrive. That calls for a max-heap.
Python's heapq is a min-heap. Push -s for each stone, and negate again when you pop.

complexity.time: O(log n) per push or pop
complexity.why: A heap is a complete binary tree of height about log₂ n, and sifting moves along one root-to-leaf path. Building a heap from n values with heapify takes O(n), and n pops take O(n log n).

mistakes: Forgetting that Python's heapq is a min-heap only. For a max-heap, store negated values.
Assuming the heap's array is sorted. Only heap[0] is guaranteed; the rest is just partly ordered.
Sorting again after every insert instead of using a heap, which turns O(log n) into O(n log n).
Sifting down towards the first smaller child rather than the smallest child, which breaks the heap rule.

quiz.question: In an array-backed heap, where are the children of index i?
quiz.explain: The tree is stored level by level, so node i's children sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent at (i − 1) / 2 rounded down.

quiz.question: What does popping a min-heap of n values cost?
quiz.explain: Reading the root is O(1), but refilling it means sifting the last value down one path of length about log n.

quiz.question: How do you get a max-heap from Python's heapq?
choices: Push negated values and negate on the way out
Sort the list in reverse first
quiz.explain: heapq only builds min-heaps. Negating flips the order, so the largest value comes out first.

interviewTip: Say which heap you need and why before coding: “a max-heap, because I keep taking the largest”. In Python, mention the negation trick; in JavaScript, say you will write a small heap or use a sorted structure.
